title: Networked low-cost passive sensing: dismounted acoustic/RF detection of Group 1-2 and RF-silent UAS, and SDR-based interference/rogue-emitter geolocation for installations, ranges and shared bands
problem: Dismounted small units have no cheap, non-emitting, TAK-connected way to detect, locate and classify Group 1-2 drones (including fiber-optic or autonomous RF-silent ones), and installations, ranges and shared-spectrum bands lack affordable persistent detection and geolocation of interference and unknown emitters short of premium monitoring networks or a handful of newly capitalized passive-sensing vendors.
echelons: tactical unit (dismounted squad/platoon, forward CP, convoy)

user.exact_role: Primary: squad/platoon leader or designated C-sUAS soldier on a dismounted patrol or at a forward command post who needs a bearing-and-class alert on a phone/ATAK without radiating. Secondary: installation spectrum manager, range control officer, security forces/base defense operations center operator and JIATF-401 C-UAS cell analyst who must find interference sources and RF-silent aircraft over a base or range.
organization_examples: U.S. Army infantry and cavalry platoons in transforming-in-contact divisions (25th ID, 101st, 2CR, 1/3 ID per S12 notes on S2AS units)
DEVCOM C5ISR Center (RFI author, Aberdeen Proving Ground)
USNORTHCOM Falcon Peak exercise cells and Joint Task Force Southern Border
Installation spectrum managers and range control at Army/DAF installations; DoD CIO spectrum-sharing analysts; secondary FCC/NTIA enforcement and CBRS/5G operators
Allied: Polish Eastern Shield C-UAS testers, Norwegian Armed Forces (Discovair buyer), Romania (JIATF-401 marketplace access)

current_workflow: Soldier hears or sees a drone, or an installation receives an interference complaint or a drone-sighting report.
Dismounted: handheld/vehicle RF detectors (DroneShield, Dedrone, Guardian RF Scout) alert only if the drone emits a recognizable control/video link; fiber-optic and autonomous drones give no RF cue.

Installation: a technician drives out with a handheld analyzer or a rented CRFS/R&S node and triangulates manually over hours to days; drone detection runs on a separate C-UAS stack (Hidden Level AMS, Dedrone, radar) with its own dashboard.
Alerts are shouted, radioed or pushed into ATAK/FAAD C2/Lattice when a C2 link and an adapter exist; Falcon Peak 26.2 now uses Anduril Lattice as the baseline C2 against which sensors are measured.
Engagement or resolution: small arms/handheld effector for drones; report to spectrum manager and slow escalation for interference; after-action data rarely feeds a shared signature library.
current_solution: Vehicle- or site-mounted active radars (SRC, Echodyne, MatrixSpace), emitter-dependent RF detectors (DroneShield, Dedrone/Axon, Guardian RF, Sentrycs), passive RF/passive radar networks for installations (Hidden Level, now scaling under a $100M OTA ceiling), NATO-fielded directional acoustic arrays (Squarehead Discovair, sold via DroneShield and UNIFY.C2 partnerships), premium spectrum-monitoring networks (CRFS RFeye, Rohde & Schwarz, Keysight), Distributed Spectrum edge-AI RF sensors, hobbyist-grade coherent DF (KrakenSDR, about EUR 1,063 retail), and improvised Ukrainian phone/microphone acoustic nets (Sky Fortress, Zvook, FENEK).
failure: RF detection fails on RF-silent and fiber-optic drones; radars emit, cost tens of thousands per unit and are not dismount-portable; acoustic detection is either a large fixed array, an allied product without a U.S. program of record, or an unproven low-SWaP concept the Army only began market research on in January 2026 (range, wind/battle-noise false alarms and classification at platoon scale are unproven in public evidence); installation spectrum monitoring is priced per premium node and split into separate stacks for interference, drones and EW, so persistent low-cost geolocation across a whole base or shared band is rarely funded.

evidence.claim: DEVCOM C5ISR Center issued an RFI on 2026-01-14 (responses due 2026-02-17) for a low-SWaP dismounted system that passively detects Group 1-2 UAS acoustically, determines bearing/location/classification, notifies the soldier on a smart device and displays the track in TAK, to inform requirements and prototyping. No award or follow-on found in public evidence.
evidence.source_title: Army seeks acoustic detection systems to counter small drones (DefenseScoop); US Army publishes RFI for small drone acoustic detection systems (Unmanned Airspace)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: The Department of War awarded Hidden Level a $100M Other Transaction Agreement (announced 2026-07-30/08-05) to deploy passive RF/passive-radar sensors over bases, test ranges and border sections, explicitly citing detection of RF-silent drones and following T-REX 25.2 and Falcon Peak 25.2 performance. $100M is a ceiling-type figure; obligated amount is not public and deployment scale is unproven.
evidence.source_title: Department of War Awards Hidden Level $100 Million OTA to Scale Passive Sensing Technology (PR Newswire); Hidden Level Secures $100M US Military Contract (The Defense Post)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: DIU, JIATF-401, USNORTHCOM and the Army ran a C-sUAS Low-Cost Sensing Challenge: 115 submissions, 10 finalists tested live at Falcon Peak 25.2 across passive RF, active radar, acoustic, EO/IR and hybrid modalities, judged on detection, classification, localization, scalability, cost and integration readiness; MatrixSpace won $500K and Guardian RF, Hidden Level and Teledyne FLIR Defense received $100K each (announced Dec 2025). Prize selection is not production.
evidence.source_title: DIU, JIATF-401, USNORTHCOM, US Army announce winner for C-UAS Low-Cost Sensing (diu.mil); DIU Announces MatrixSpace Winner (DroneLife)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: JIATF-401's counter-UAS marketplace (IOC announced 2026-02-24, hosted on the Common Hardware Systems electronic catalog under an existing IDIQ) completed four initial purchases totaling about $13M for CENTCOM, homeland-defense services and JTF Southern Border, including sensor systems, radars and EW systems; the catalog held about a dozen systems. Small dollar values; marketplace listing is not the same as fielding.
evidence.source_title: Counter-UAS Marketplace Streamlines Acquisition, First Purchases Total $13 Million (war.gov); JIATF 401 Makes 1st Purchases Via Counter-UAS Marketplace (ExecutiveGov)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: JIATF-401's 2026 Counter-sUAS Quick Reference Guide (2026-09-08) names acoustic detection as one of four sensor categories in a layered approach alongside radar, EO/IR and RF sensing, and emphasizes privacy protections for domestic sensing - a joint owner formally recognizes the modality but has not published an acoustic requirement or program of record.
evidence.source_title: Joint Interagency Task Force 401 2026 Counter-Small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Quick Reference Guide (media.defense.gov); JIATF-401 Issues Counter-Drone Sensor Guide (Inside Unmanned Systems)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: Ukraine fielded very large low-cost acoustic networks (Sky Fortress reported at ~14,000 sensors built for roughly $400-1,000 each; Zvook covering ~5% of territory; FENEK) that cue air defenses against Shahed-class and small UAS; an official U.S. Army article now documents these as emerging technology. Reported interception-rate claims (e.g., 80 of 84) are media/advocate figures, not independently verified.
evidence.source_title: Listening to the Sky: Acoustic Drone Detection Systems - Ukraine & Emerging Technologies (army.mil); Sky Fortress (united24media); NATO shows interest in Ukrainian acoustic detection networks (Militarnyi)
evidence.label: FACT (scale and cost figures MEDIUM; effectiveness claims INFERENCE)

evidence.claim: Poland tested seven acoustic drone-detection systems at Ustka on 2026-04-22 under Eastern Shield (including Squarehead Discovair G2+; Poland reported 715+ submissions and 36 solutions tested); Squarehead reported a Norwegian Armed Forces contract for Discovair co-located with C-RAM radars (mid-2025); Squarehead partnered with DroneShield and UNIFY.C2 for U.S./allied distribution; Guardian RF partnered with Picogrid for a Space Force base-defense integration (2026-02-25); Distributed Spectrum raised a $25M Series A (2025-03) on low-cost edge-AI RF sensors. Many vendors hold pieces; none has a public U.S. dismounted-acoustic program of record.
evidence.source_title: Poland tests Norwegian acoustic drone detector (Defence Blog); UNIFY.C2 and Squarehead partner (EIN Presswire); Picogrid, Guardian RF partner (The Defense Post); Distributed Spectrum Series A (Defense Tech Signals)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: GAO-26-107873 (2026-06-05) found DoD and NTIA spectrum-sharing studies lacked transparency and collaboration; shared federal bands (e.g., CBRS with ESC sensors) depend on monitoring and interference resolution capacity, which implies sustained demand for affordable persistent sensing. NTIA/NIST earlier defined a tiered COTS-sensor Spectrum Monitoring Pilot Program (high to ultra-low cost tiers) - a decade-old design pattern that never became a large procurement.
evidence.source_title: GAO-26-107873 Spectrum Sharing: DOD and NTIA collaboration (gao.gov); An Overview of the NTIA/NIST Spectrum Monitoring Pilot Program (NIST)
evidence.label: FACT (demand implication is INFERENCE)

evidence.claim: The Army moved from a REWSI call for solutions (April 2026) to roughly $196M in spectrum-sensor production contracts to two non-traditional vendors within five months (Research Innovations $96.9M, 2026-09-03), showing that cheap, numerous spectrum sensors are now bought at production scale outside programs of record - but those awards went to already-selected vendors, not to new entrants.
evidence.source_title: Army awards $196M sensor production contracts for electronic warfare (DefenseScoop); Army taps Research Innovations for mobile spectrum detection (Washington Technology)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: Emitter-based RF detectors cannot detect fiber-optic or autonomous RF-silent drones by construction; the Hidden Level OTA justification and the C5ISR acoustic RFI both exist because of this gap. That the RF-silent share of the threat is growing is INFERENCE from Ukraine reporting, not a quantified U.S. figure.
evidence.source_title: Passive Radar That Catches RF-Silent Drones Earns $100M Pentagon Contract (TechTimes); C5ISR RFI (DefenseScoop)
evidence.label: INFERENCE

evidence.claim: Commodity coherent direction-finding hardware (KrakenSDR: five phase-coherent RTL-SDR channels, 100-1000 MHz, internal calibration, EUR 1,063 retail with cloud multi-station bearing fusion 'RDF Pro') exists and is used by hobbyists and reportedly some units, so the barrier to low-cost networked geolocation is calibration, time-sync, classification and false-alarm software rather than RF front-end hardware. Military use is RECALL - not re-verified this session.
evidence.source_title: KrakenSDR (Crowd Supply); KrakenSDR receiver pack (Passion Radio); KrakenSDR review 2026 (SDR Store)
evidence.label: FACT (hardware) / INFERENCE (barrier is software)

evidence.claim: Falcon Peak 26.2 (Sept 2026) is the first iteration in which USNORTHCOM used Anduril Lattice as the digital backbone and baseline against which all commercial sensor-to-shooter C-UAS assets are measured; JIATF-401 selected Lattice as a key tactical C-UAS C2 via an $87M contract under the Army Enterprise Agreement with Anduril - any new sensor must integrate to Lattice/FAAD C2 rather than sell its own C2.
evidence.source_title: What's unique about Northcom's Falcon Peak 26.2 counter-drone exercise (DefenseScoop)
evidence.label: FACT

evidence.claim: Aurora Insight's commercial RF-mapping business exited to Maxar (Jan 2023) and later to HawkEye 360 without reaching independent scale, a warning that data-only spectrum plays without a defense program anchor struggle to fund themselves.
evidence.source_title: Aurora Insight supplier profile (Sky Brokers); companies/B09 record
evidence.label: FACT

why_existing_startups_havent_solved: The dismounted acoustic requirement only crystallized in the U.S. in January 2026 (C5ISR RFI) and still has no published requirement, budget line or program of record; the installation problem is being solved by government-selected vendors (Hidden Level under a $100M OTA ceiling; MatrixSpace, Guardian RF, Teledyne FLIR as DIU challenge top performers; Research Innovations under REWSI) who were chosen through year-long test cycles (Falcon Peak, T-REX, DIU challenge) that a new entrant must also pass. Acoustic and passive-RF performance depends on large labeled signature datasets collected in realistic wind, vehicle and gunfire noise, which only deployed vendors and Ukraine hold; incumbents bundle detection into C2 suites (Anduril Lattice is now the Falcon Peak baseline), so a sensor-only startup is a component supplier to someone else's architecture. Allied acoustic leaders (Squarehead) enter the U.S. through partners (DroneShield, UNIFY.C2) rather than leaving space open. The dual-use spectrum-monitoring side is price-sensitive and, per Aurora Insight, has not sustained a standalone data business.
technical_wedge: Not the sensor hardware. The defensible wedge is the software and network layer: (1) on-device ML classification and bearing estimation that runs on a sub-$1,500 BOM node (MEMS microphone array plus one coherent SDR on a Jetson-class or smartphone-class processor), (2) self-calibrating multi-node TDOA/AoA fusion that turns many cheap, imperfectly synchronized nodes into a track with an honest confidence, (3) a false-alarm model trained on a self-collected, continuously growing signature library (Part 107 drones, fiber-optic FPV analogs, vehicles, generators, gunfire ranges), and (4) native CoT/TAK plugin and Lattice/FAAD C2 adapters so the output lands where JIATF-401 and USNORTHCOM already look. The same TDOA/AoA engine serves interference and rogue-emitter geolocation for installation spectrum managers and shared-band operators, giving a dual-use commercial path (CBRS/5G operators, range control, event security).

mvp.what: A 6-8 node network of commodity nodes (4-8 MEMS microphones + one 5-channel coherent SDR + edge processor + GPS/PTP time sync, under $1,500 BOM each) with an on-device drone classifier and a central self-calibrating fusion service, publishing tracks and emitter geolocations as Cursor-on-Target into an ATAK plugin and a web dashboard.
mvp.demonstrable_in_3_6_months: On a university field or an FAA-legal test range: detect and classify a Part 107 quadcopter and a fixed-wing sUAS in silent (RF-off, pre-programmed) flight at a stated range with published probability-of-detection and false-alarm curves in wind and traffic noise, and geolocate a cooperative test transmitter (licensed amateur or ISM band) to a stated CEP using the same nodes; show the tracks arriving in ATAK on a phone.
mvp.what_it_must_prove: That a cheap networked node achieves usable range (hundreds of meters for Group 1 in realistic noise) with a false-alarm rate a squad would tolerate, that many cheap nodes fuse into a track at least as good as one expensive sensor, that the system stays under dismount SWaP limits, and that it integrates through TAK/CoT without a bespoke C2. It must also prove the team can generate its own labeled data flywheel.

data_requirement.what: Labeled acoustic signatures of Group 1-2 drones (multirotor, fixed-wing, fiber-optic FPV analogs) across distances, aspects, wind, terrain and background noise (vehicles, generators, gunfire, urban); labeled RF captures of drone links, jammers and common installation emitters; multi-node time-synchronized recordings for TDOA calibration.
data_requirement.legally_realistically_obtainable: Yes for the MVP: self-collected with Part 107 drones on private land, plus public datasets (DroneAudioDataset-type academic corpora, ITS/NTIA spectrum recordings) and synthetic augmentation. Military threat signatures (specific adversary drones, Ukrainian field recordings) are not public and would come only through a CRADA with C5ISR Center/ARL, a JIATF-401 test event, or an allied partner; Ukraine-derived data is held by vendors such as Guardian RF and Zvook.

entry_vehicle.eligibility_notes: SBIR/STTR requires the small business to be more than 50% owned and controlled by U.S. citizens or permanent residents (or by other qualifying U.S. small businesses) and to perform the work in the United States; an Indonesian founder who is not a U.S. person holding a large equity stake could break SBIR eligibility and would require a cap-table structure reviewed by counsel. OTs, CSOs, DIU awards and prize challenges do not carry the SBIR ownership rule but do carry ITAR/EAR deemed-export exposure once the acoustic/RF sensor or its technical data is 'specially designed' for a military application (USML Category XI is the usual concern; commodity SDR and microphones are generally EAR - needs counsel, not a legal judgment here). Non-U.S.-person founders may also be excluded from CUI/controlled test data at Falcon Peak-type events. Any future facility clearance triggers FOCI review. Allied markets (Poland, Norway, Germany) have their own export and national-security screening.

incumbent_response.could_anduril_palantir_l3harris_add_it: Yes. Hidden Level or Anduril can add microphone arrays to existing nodes; DroneShield already resells Squarehead acoustics; Anduril controls Lattice and can prioritize its own sensors; L3Harris sells Drone Guardian; Research Innovations holds the Army spectrum-sensor production lane. The acoustic and coherent-SDR hardware is commodity, so the only slow-to-copy asset is a labeled signature corpus and a tested false-alarm model.
incumbent_response.why_startup_still_wins_or_reject: A startup wins only if it is the best software layer for cheap nodes (fusion, calibration, classification, TAK-native workflow) and accumulates a data flywheel faster than sensor incumbents care to on the low-margin dismounted end, or if it targets the neglected dual-use installation/shared-band interference niche where C-UAS vendors do not sell. As a hardware node vendor competing head-on with Hidden Level, MatrixSpace and Guardian RF on $250K, reject.

regulatory_burden.explanation: The MVP is unclassified and built from commercial parts, and Part 107 flights and receive-only SDR use are legal in the U.S. But once a node is adapted for military C-UAS (ruggedized, integrated with FAAD C2/Lattice, trained on government threat data) it may be treated as a defense article or defense service under USML Category XI (military electronics), making technical-data sharing with a non-U.S.-person founder or foreign employee a deemed export requiring a license. Domestic C-UAS sensing also intersects 18 U.S.C. 3121-style pen-register and Wiretap Act concerns for RF collection and privacy guidance in the JIATF-401 sensor guide; interference geolocation for civil users must respect FCC rules on receiving and disclosing communications content. Any facility clearance or classified threat library later triggers FOCI mitigation. None of this is a legal judgment; all of it needs counsel.
regulatory_burden.non_us_person_founder_note: The Indonesian founder (not assumed a U.S. person) is the main structural risk: SBIR/STTR ownership and control rules, ITAR deemed-export limits on technical data, exclusion from CUI at test events, and FOCI review if a clearance is ever needed. Mitigations to review with counsel: keep the company's controlled technical data segregated, have the German founder (expected permanent resident) and U.S. hires hold the controlled roles, structure the cap table for SBIR eligibility, and pursue OT/CSO/prize vehicles that do not have SBIR ownership rules while the immigration status resolves.

dual_use_potential.explanation: The interference/rogue-emitter geolocation engine sells to installation spectrum managers, CBRS/5G operators, satellite ground stations, event and critical-infrastructure security and regulators, and the same nodes can detect drones over stadiums, prisons and airports. But Aurora Insight's failure to scale commercial spectrum mapping and the price sensitivity of regulators show the civil market is real but thin; defense C-UAS demand is the anchor.

defensibility.explanation: Hardware is commodity and copyable; what compounds is the labeled acoustic/RF signature corpus collected from every deployed node, the calibrated false-alarm models, the certified TAK/Lattice/FAAD adapters, an RMF-accredited fusion service, and evaluator trust earned at Falcon Peak/T-REX/Eastern Shield. Network effects are weak; deployment footprint matters because each installed node improves the models and raises replacement cost.

why_now: (1) Fiber-optic and autonomous RF-silent drones proliferated in Ukraine from 2024, breaking the RF-detector assumption and prompting the Hidden Level OTA and the C5ISR acoustic RFI (Jan 2026); (2) JIATF-401 (Aug 2025), its CSO (Feb 2026) and marketplace (Feb-Apr 2026) created a joint buyer with faster money and a DIU low-cost sensing challenge that explicitly scores cost and scalability; (3) Ukraine proved 14,000-node acoustic networks at $400-1,000 per node and the U.S. Army now publishes about them; (4) edge processors, MEMS arrays and coherent multi-channel SDRs (KrakenSDR at ~EUR 1,000) make a sub-$1,500 node feasible; (5) shared-spectrum policy (GAO-26-107873, CBRS/mid-band sharing) needs monitoring capacity; (6) Army REWSI showed non-traditional spectrum-sensor vendors can reach production within months.
killer_risk: The field already contains four government-selected, funded vendors (Hidden Level with a $100M OTA ceiling, MatrixSpace as DIU winner, Guardian RF, Squarehead via DroneShield/UNIFY.C2) plus Anduril owning the C2 baseline, and the dismounted acoustic problem is physics-limited (Group 1 quadcopter detection ranges of a few hundred meters degrade sharply in wind and battle noise - RECALL, MEDIUM), so a $250K two-founder team faces a hardware-intensive race it cannot fund through the year-long test cycles, with ITAR deemed-export exposure for its non-U.S.-person founder. If the Army's RFI produces no funded requirement, the dismounted market stays a prize-and-pilot market.

allied_extension: Yes, materially. Allied demand for cheap acoustic C-UAS is more concrete than U.S. demand: Poland tested seven acoustic systems under Eastern Shield with a multi-billion 2026 drone/anti-drone budget, Norway contracted Discovair, NATO has shown interest in Ukrainian acoustic networks, and Romania gained JIATF-401 marketplace access. A German founder gives a natural path to Bundeswehr/NATO DIANA and to European frontline states that buy faster and with fewer U.S.-person constraints, and an EU-based entity could hold the hardware while a U.S. entity sells software. The counterweights: Squarehead already owns the European acoustic lane, national procurement is fragmented, and a split U.S./EU structure adds export-control complexity in both directions.
